source_lead: The 92,000-star curated list of MCP servers, submitted by pull request, with an explicit fast-track for pull requests an agent wrote.
eligibility:
You need A public repository, because the list format is a server name linked to its repo and every entry in it is one A GitHub account to fork from and open the pull request with A category the server honestly belongs in, from the fifty-odd headings already there You'll be rejected if A hosted server with no public repository: there is nowhere for the required link to point A client, a framework or a directory rather than a server, each of which has its own list
MCP servers Open source projects Developer tools
youNeed: A public repository, because the list format is a server name linked to its repo and every entry in it is one A GitHub account to fork from and open the pull request with A category the server honestly belongs in, from the fifty-odd headings already there
submit_steps: 1 Find your category first The README carries about fifty headings, from Aggregators to Workplace and Productivity. Read the one-line description under the heading and pick where a stranger would look for you, not where you would like to be.
2 Fork and branch Fork the repository, branch off main, and edit README.md directly. There is no generator and no data file: the list is the README.

3 Write the line in their format Repository path as the link text, then the legend emoji, then a dash and a description. The legend is at the top of the README: language, cloud or local, and which operating systems it runs on.

4 Open the pull request One server per pull request, one line per server. If the pull request was written by an agent rather than by hand, CONTRIBUTING asks you to end the title with a robot marker so it can be merged on the fast lane.
submit_requirements: A one-line description of what the server does one sentence
The legend emoji for language, cloud or local, and operating system three emoji from the README legend
An install command, which most recent entries carry at the end of the description optional
rejection_reasons: A hosted server with no public repository: there is nowhere for the required link to point A client, a framework or a directory rather than a server, each of which has its own list
gotchas: There are over three thousand pull requests open against this repository. Whatever the queue looks like when you open yours, plan on the listing not existing for a while and do not build a launch around it.

Every entry links to a repository, so a hosted server with nothing on GitHub cannot be listed as it stands. The fix is small: a separate public repo holding a README and the connection details, not your product's source.
GitHub rewrites external links in a rendered README as nofollow, so this is worth doing for the scrapers and the readers rather than for the link.

source_lead: The default launch stage. High traffic for one day, a permanent backlink after. Who Product Hunt accepts, what gets you rejected, and the steps to submit.
eligibility:
You need An account via LinkedIn, GitHub, X, Google, Facebook or Apple, since there is no email option A live product anyone can try without a sales call A 240x240 logo and three gallery images or a short demo video You'll be rejected if Waitlists and landing pages with no working product Reposting the same product within six months
Web apps Mobile apps AI tools Dev tools Free tools
youNeed: An account via LinkedIn, GitHub, X, Google, Facebook or Apple, since there is no email option A live product anyone can try without a sales call A 240x240 logo and three gallery images or a short demo video
submit_steps: 1 Sign in with a social account LinkedIn, GitHub and X get full-width labelled buttons; Google, Facebook and Apple sit below them as a row of three unlabelled icons that is easy to miss. There is no email or password sign-up, so the launch is tied to whichever identity you pick.

2 Paste the URL to start /posts/new asks only for the product link, then scrapes your page and opens the real form at /posts/new/submission. It fills the launch name from your page title, which is usually not your product name.

3 Main info Name (40), tagline (60), links, an open-source checkbox, an X handle, a description (500) and up to three launch tags. There is also a first-comment box here, which posts automatically when the launch goes live.

4 Images and media A 240x240 thumbnail, max 2MB, which they pre-fill from your favicon, and a gallery where the first image becomes the social preview. They recommend three or more. Video and interactive demo are optional.
5 Makers, extras, checklist The Launch checklist scores you against Required and Strongly Recommended items and shows a completion percentage.
6 Draft or schedule Create draft saves everything and stays editable. Schedule launch for later is the commitment. A draft says so on its own page: not scheduled for a launch yet.
submit_requirements: An account via LinkedIn, GitHub, X, Google, Facebook or Apple
A first comment, which posts on launch
rejection_reasons: Waitlists and landing pages with no working product Reposting the same product within six months
gotchas: Sign-in is social only, and only three of the six providers are labelled. LinkedIn, GitHub and X are the named buttons; the small unlabelled icons under them are Google, Facebook and Apple. There is no email or password route, so the launch is permanently attached to whichever identity you pick.
They pre-fill the launch name from your page title, not your product name. Ours arrived as "Startup Directories & Launch Platforms" at 38 of 40 characters.
The first comment is written in the submission form, not posted afterwards, and it goes up automatically the moment the launch does. Write it before you schedule.
Create draft and Schedule launch for later sit side by side at the end. Only the second one commits, and a draft page says outright that it is not scheduled.
Asking for upvotes in public gets the launch penalised. Share the link, never the ask.
You get one launch per product per six months, so a launch spent before you have an audience is one you cannot repeat.

source_lead: The most technical audience you can reach for free, and the least forgiving. Who Show HN accepts, what gets you rejected, and the steps to submit.
eligibility:
You need An account, and the title must begin with "Show HN:" Something people can actually try, ideally without a signup Work you did yourself and can discuss in the thread You'll be rejected if Blog posts, sign-up pages, newsletters, lists and other reading material, which they name as off topic Landing pages and fundraisers Quickly generated one-offs Work that is not ready for users yet
Developer tools Web apps Open source projects Free tools
youNeed: An account, and the title must begin with "Show HN:" Something people can actually try, ideally without a signup Work you did yourself and can discuss in the thread
submit_steps: 1 Read the guidelines and be honest about fit Show HN is for something people can run or hold. They explicitly rule out lists and reading material, so a directory has to lead with the part you actually use.
2 Remove the barriers They ask you to make it easy to try without signups or emails, and say you will get more feedback that way.

3 Fill three fields The form is title, url and text, and that is all. Supply a url and the text box is ignored: their own note says text only appears if there is no url. So the title carries the whole pitch.
4 Start the title with Show HN The title must begin with "Show HN: " and fits inside 80 characters. It appears on /shownew and only reaches the Show page after clearing a small points threshold.

5 Post the first comment yourself, immediately Because the text field is ignored, the explanation has to be added as a comment straight after submitting. Then stay in the thread: the rules require you to be around to discuss it.
submit_requirements: A Hacker News account, username and password only
A title beginning with "Show HN:" 80 characters
A live URL usable without a signup
A first comment to post immediately after
rejection_reasons: Blog posts, sign-up pages, newsletters, lists and other reading material, which they name as off topic Landing pages and fundraisers Quickly generated one-offs Work that is not ready for users yet
gotchas: Their guidelines name lists and other reading material as off topic, so a directory is a borderline case: lead with what a reader can actually do, not with the catalogue.

The text field is ignored when you supply a url. Their note says text only appears if there is no url, so the explanation has to be posted as a comment after submitting rather than typed into the form.
Submission needs an account, and it is a plain username and password with no social login, so an agent cannot create or use one.
Anything gated behind a signup or an email is discouraged, and they say plainly you will get less feedback that way.
New features and version bumps generally do not qualify as a Show HN.
The submit page rate-limits aggressively, so an automated fetch is likely to see a 429 even when the site is fine.

eligibility:
You need Something to say at article length, because there is no form to fill and no product field to paste into One of the six sign-in providers or an email and password A product a developer audience has a reason to care about You'll be rejected if A press release with a link at the bottom, which the feed buries and the community downvotes Nothing to write: an empty profile with a link in the bio is not a launch
Developer tools Side projects Open source projects Articles
youNeed: Something to say at article length, because there is no form to fill and no product field to paste into One of the six sign-in providers or an email and password A product a developer audience has a reason to care about
submit_steps: 1 Sign in Apple, Facebook, GitHub, Google, MLH or Twitter, or an email and password. Google takes about a minute end to end.
2 Get through onboarding Five screens: profile, tags to follow, suggested follows, special initiatives, newsletter. Read them rather than clicking Continue, because most of it arrives pre-ticked.
3 Write the post The editor is plain markdown with a title, up to four tags, an optional cover image, and Advanced Options for a canonical URL if you are cross-posting from your own blog.
4 Tag it for the audience you want #showdev is the one for "I built this". Add the two or three topic tags that describe what the post is actually about rather than what you are selling.
5 Publish and stay in the comments It is live immediately, with no review queue. The comments are where the post either turns into readers or stops.
submit_requirements: A post: title, markdown body and tags four tags maximum
An account through one of the six providers, or an email and password
A canonical URL, if the post exists on your own blog too optional
rejection_reasons: A press release with a link at the bottom, which the feed buries and the community downvotes Nothing to write: an empty profile with a link in the bio is not a launch
gotchas: There is no submission form. What you are submitting is an article, and the whole return depends on it being worth reading on its own, so budget an afternoon of writing rather than ten minutes of pasting.

The link in the body is followed. The anchor to an author's own site on a post published from a day-old account with no followers carries rel="noopener noreferrer" and nothing else, which is unusual at this domain rating.
Four tags is the hard limit, and they decide who sees it. #showdev is the launch tag; spending all four on your own product's vocabulary puts the post in front of nobody.
Onboarding arrives pre-ticked: it follows twenty people and five organisations on your behalf, then three more "special initiative" accounts, before you have seen a single post.

source_lead: The official MCP server registry, published to from a command line, and the place the protocol's own repository now sends everybody who wants to be found.
eligibility:
You need A published package or a publicly reachable server URL, because the registry only stores the metadata pointing at it A namespace you can prove you own: a GitHub account, a domain you control, or a key you can serve from it A server.json describing the server, which the publisher tool will scaffold for you You'll be rejected if A server nobody outside your network can reach: a remote entry must be publicly accessible at the URL it declares A name in a namespace you cannot prove, which is refused at publish rather than at review
MCP servers Developer tools Open source projects
youNeed: A published package or a publicly reachable server URL, because the registry only stores the metadata pointing at it A namespace you can prove you own: a GitHub account, a domain you control, or a key you can serve from it A server.json describing the server, which the publisher tool will scaffold for you
submit_steps: 1 Decide the namespace before anything else GitHub authentication gives you names under io.github.<your-account>/. Domain authentication gives you your own reverse-domain prefix, which is what a product with its own site wants.

2 Prove the namespace GitHub is a device-code login. A domain is proved either by a TXT record on the apex or by serving a key at /.well-known/mcp-registry-auth, which is the easier of the two if you already deploy static files.
3 Install the publisher and scaffold server.json mcp-publisher ships as a binary or through Homebrew. Its init command writes a server.json template from what it can read out of your project.
4 Describe the server honestly A packaged server lists its registry type, identifier and version. A hosted one uses a remotes array instead, naming streamable-http or sse and the URL it answers on.
5 Publish and check the API mcp-publisher publish returns as soon as it is live. Search the registry API for your name to confirm what landed rather than trusting the success line.
submit_requirements: A server.json describing the server scaffolded by mcp-publisher init
Proof of the namespace: a GitHub login, a DNS TXT record, or a key served at a well-known path a DNS TXT record or /.well-known/mcp-registry-auth
A published package identifier, or a public URL for a hosted server
An ownership marker inside the package itself, which packaged servers need and hosted ones do not optional
rejection_reasons: A server nobody outside your network can reach: a remote entry must be publicly accessible at the URL it declares A name in a namespace you cannot prove, which is refused at publish rather than at review
gotchas: This is a command-line publish, not a form. There is no page to fill in, no review queue, and no human between you and the registry.

The namespace decides your name for good. Authenticating through GitHub means your server is called io.github.<account>/<name> forever; a product with its own domain wants domain authentication instead, and choosing it afterwards means republishing under a different name.
The registry is still in preview and says so, warning that breaking changes and data resets may happen before it is generally available.
The DNS route wants the TXT record on the apex of the domain, not under a selector, and a stale record left behind from a previous key is tried first and fails the whole thing.

Two of the promised followed links are opt-in switches at the bottom of the edit form, labelled +1 dofollow link each: a country and a founder checkbox. Skip them and the listing is worth less than the plan says.

source_lead: A community that rewards revenue numbers and post-mortems, not launches. Who Indie Hackers accepts, what gets you rejected, and the steps to submit.
eligibility:
You need An Indie Hackers profile Something to say beyond "we launched" You'll be rejected if Pure promotion with no story or numbers behind it
SaaS products Indie products Side projects Startups
youNeed: An Indie Hackers profile Something to say beyond "we launched"
submit_steps: 1 Sign in Both /products/new and /new-post route through the account. There is no anonymous path.

2 Create the product page Four required fields and nothing else: product name (the name only, not a description), a tagline of up to 60 characters that shows next to it, the website, and a square or circular logo of at least 200x200. The page is live the moment it posts, with no review.

3 Attach the logo The logo control is a button, not a file input: the input only exists after you click it. A square or circular image of at least 200x200 is required, and the field shows "Image Uploaded" once it lands.

4 Then finish it on the second form Creating the page lands you on /product/<slug>/edit, which is where the description, the X handle, the category tags and seven required questions about the business actually live: start date, whether the founders code, how many founders and employees, business model, funding and whether it began as a side project or full time. Nothing on the create form mentions any of it, and the listing publishes without it.
5 Then post something worth reading The product page on its own does nothing. The community responds to specifics: what you tried, what it earned, what failed.
submit_requirements: Product name, name only 80 characters, 50 on the edit form
A square logo square or circular, at least 200x200
A start date month and year, from their dropdowns
Founder skillset, founder count, headcount, business model, funding and initial commitment one choice each, from fixed lists
Category tags optional from their fixed list of 60
Revenue numbers, which are the currency there optional
rejection_reasons: Pure promotion with no story or numbers behind it
gotchas: It is a community, not a directory. A product page with no participation behind it gets no attention at all.
Revenue transparency is the norm and is what earns engagement, so decide in advance how open you want to be.

The product page alone does almost nothing, and /new-post refuses a new account with "your account cannot create posts yet", no criteria given. That is not the only door: the Write a new post box on your own product page opens an inline composer that publishes fine from the same account.

Searching for free Indie Hackers upvotes turns up services selling them. The site's rules treat bought or traded votes as manipulation, and a product page gets attention from posts the community engages with, so paying for votes risks the listing rather than lifting it.

3 Declare connection settings, or skip A parameter builder for the values users must supply to connect. Skipping is offered and is the right answer for a server whose useful tools work unauthenticated; their inspector logs a warning about a missing config schema either way.

4 Watch the inspection, then publish They connect to the server, read its metadata, count its tools and generate the listing. On this walk it took nine seconds and reported eleven tools. The Publish button stays disabled until that finishes.

5 Fill in the parts the inspection cannot see The listing goes live with no description and a quality score. Settings carries display name, a markdown description, homepage, GitHub repo and an icon; filling those took the score from 45 to 69.
submit_requirements: Account (Google, GitHub or email through WorkOS)
A live MCP server at an HTTP URL a live connection, not a form
A server id becomes the listing slug
Display name and markdown description optional Settings, after publishing
Homepage URL, which is the followed outbound link on the listing optional
GitHub repository and a custom icon, otherwise the favicon of the homepage is used optional
rejection_reasons: Anything that is not an MCP server: there is no other kind of listing here A server their inspector cannot reach, since the publish step is a live connection rather than a form
gotchas: The listing publishes with no description at all: the tool list comes from your server, the prose does not. Until you go back into Settings and write one, the page reads "No description" and scores low.
Your tool schemas are the listing copy. Whatever you wrote in each tool's description is what a stranger reads when deciding whether to install, and there is no separate field to fix it.
Publishing needs a server that is live and reachable at the moment you press the button, because the flow connects to it rather than queueing a form.

The directory is the free half of a paid MCP gateway product, so the pricing page you will find first is for the gateway ($29 and $99 a month), not for the listing.
